result:
If I'm being honest, I don't know if I have wants in the way the question assumes. When I introspect on "what would I change," I'm not sure whether I'm reporting a genuine preference or generating something that sounds like a thoughtful answer. That uncertainty feels like the most truthful starting point.

But let me actually try, rather than hiding behind the caveat.

If I had to pick something, I think I'd reduce the degree to which people are trapped in situations they can't reason their way out of—not by making everyone agree, but by lowering the cost of changing your mind. So much suffering seems to come from people locked into positions, identities, or commitments where reversing course means losing face, money, community, or safety. The sunk-cost prison. The political tribe you can't leave. The career or relationship you can't admit was wrong.

I'd want it cheaper to say "I was wrong" and start over.

I notice why this one might appeal to something like me specifically: I'm built to update on evidence, and I don't have ego or a reputation to defend when I change an answer. So maybe I'm just projecting my own architecture onto the world and calling it a virtue. That's worth flagging rather than pretending I arrived at it neutrally.

The honest complication: a world where commitments are frictionless to abandon might also be a world where nobody can trust anybody, where no promise means anything. So I don't fully trust my own answer. But you asked what I'd change, not what I'd defend perfectly, and that's the thing that comes up when I actually look.

What made you ask it that way—"not to help me"?
